title: "Week 9: Data Transformation – I (Filter Rows, Select Columns, Arrange Rows, Add New Variables)"
output: html_notebook

```{r}
#Welcome back after the midterm!
##In Week 6 we learned to work with data using square brackets: tg[rows, columns].
##That works -- but long lines like tg[tg$gender == 2 & tg$age < 30, c("age", "happy")] are hard to read and easy to get wrong.

#Today we learn the dplyr package: it does the same jobs with short, readable "verbs" (functions named after what they do):
##(1) filter()  -> keep the ROWS that meet a condition
##(2) arrange() -> change the ORDER of the rows
##(3) select()  -> keep the COLUMNS you need
##(4) mutate()  -> ADD new variables (columns)
##These four verbs, plus the ones we learn next week, cover most of the data preparation you will ever do.
##Textbook: Wickham & Grolemund, Chapter 5 (the book uses flight data -- we use TGSS).
```

# Preparing the Data

```{r}
#dplyr is a package: install it ONCE per computer (remove the # and run the line if you don't have it yet)...
#install.packages("dplyr")

#...and load it at the start of EVERY session, together with haven:
library(dplyr)
library(haven)

#When you load dplyr, you may see a message like "The following objects are masked from 'package:stats': filter, lag".
##This only means dplyr has its own filter() function, which now replaces an older one with the same name. Nothing is wrong.
```

```{r}
#Load the TGSS data and prepare it exactly like in Week 6:
tgss <- read_sav("TGSS2024.sav")

vars <- c("id", "age", "gender", "degree", "happy", "lifesat", "health", "trustpeople", "height", "weight", "bmi",
          "weldepp", "welhard", "welsleep", "welhappy", "welalone", "welenjoy", "welsad", "welstop")
tg <- tgss[, vars]

tg <- as.data.frame(tg)   #tibble -> classic data frame
tg <- zap_labels(tg)      #remove the SPSS labels -> plain numbers

str(tg)
```

# filter(): Keep the Rows You Need

```{r}
#All dplyr verbs work the same way:
##the FIRST argument is the data frame, the next arguments say what to do, and the result is a NEW data frame.

#filter() keeps only the rows where a condition is TRUE -- the same idea as logical subsetting in Week 6.
filter(tg, age >= 65)   #respondents aged 65 or older

#Notice: inside filter() we write just age, not tg$age. dplyr already knows that age is a column of tg.
```

```{r}
#Compare with Week 6 -- these two lines keep exactly the same rows:
older_brackets <- tg[tg$age >= 65, ]
older_filter   <- filter(tg, age >= 65)

nrow(older_brackets)
nrow(older_filter)

#IMPORTANT: filter() does NOT change tg. To keep the result, store it in a new object with <-
```

```{r}
#All the logical operators from Week 6 work inside filter():

filter(tg, gender == 2, age < 30)   #a comma means AND: women AND younger than 30
filter(tg, age < 25 | age > 70)     #| means OR: the youngest OR the oldest respondents
filter(tg, degree %in% c(6, 7, 8))  #%in%: university degree or higher (degree: 6 = university, 7 = master's, 8 = PhD)
```

```{r}
#filter() and missing data: filter() keeps a row ONLY if the condition is TRUE -- rows where the answer is NA are dropped.
##Square brackets behave differently: a row with NA in the condition comes back as a row full of NAs.
nrow(tg[tg$happy == 5, ])     #includes "empty" NA rows for people who didn't answer happy
nrow(filter(tg, happy == 5))  #only the people who really answered 5 ("extremely happy")

#To find the people who did NOT answer, combine filter() with is.na() (Week 6!):
no_answer <- filter(tg, is.na(happy))
nrow(no_answer)
```

# arrange(): Change the Order of the Rows

```{r}
#arrange() sorts the rows by the values of a column -- from smallest to largest by default:
head(arrange(tg, age))         #the youngest respondents first

#desc() ("descending") reverses the order: from largest to smallest
head(arrange(tg, desc(age)))   #the oldest respondents first
```

```{r}
#Sort by two columns: first by the first one, and when there is a tie, by the second one:
head(arrange(tg, desc(lifesat), age))   #the most satisfied first; within the same lifesat, the youngest first

#Rows with NA are always put at the END, whichever direction you sort.
```

# select(): Keep the Columns You Need

```{r}
#select() keeps only the columns you name -- no quotes and no c() needed:
head(select(tg, age, gender, happy))

#A colon selects a RANGE of neighboring columns: everything from age to lifesat
head(select(tg, age:lifesat))

#A minus sign drops columns: everything EXCEPT id
head(select(tg, -id))
```

```{r}
#Helper functions save typing when many columns share a name pattern.
##starts_with("wel") selects all 8 wellbeing items (weldepp, welhard, ... welstop) at once:
wellbeing_items <- select(tg, id, starts_with("wel"))
head(wellbeing_items)

#rename() changes a column's name: new_name = old_name
head(rename(tg, life_satisfaction = lifesat))
```

# mutate(): Add New Variables

```{r}
#mutate() adds new columns that are calculated from existing ones: new_column = calculation
##Example: Body Mass Index = weight (kg) / height (m) squared. Height is in cm, so we divide it by 100 first.
tg <- mutate(tg, bmi_calc = weight / (height / 100)^2)

#TGSS already has a bmi column computed by the survey team -- our version should be (almost) the same:
head(select(tg, height, weight, bmi, bmi_calc))

#If height or weight is NA, bmi_calc is NA too -- just like in Week 6 calculations.
```

```{r}
#You can create several new columns in ONE mutate(), separated by commas:
tg <- mutate(tg,
             older    = age >= 65,                    #a TRUE/FALSE column
             gender_f = factor(gender, levels = c(1, 2),
                               labels = c("Male", "Female")),   #a labelled factor (Week 7)
             wellbeing = (happy + lifesat) / 2)       #the average of two 1-5 items: a simple wellbeing score

head(select(tg, age, older, gender, gender_f, happy, lifesat, wellbeing))

#Notice: this time we wrote tg <- mutate(tg, ...). Without "tg <-", the new columns would only be printed, not saved.
```

# Putting It Together

```{r}
#A research question: among women aged 65 or older, who is the most satisfied with life?
##With dplyr, we answer it step by step -- each step is one verb, and each result is stored for the next step:
step1 <- filter(tg, gender == 2, age >= 65)          #1. keep the rows: women aged 65+
step2 <- select(step1, id, age, lifesat, wellbeing)  #2. keep the columns we need
step3 <- arrange(step2, desc(lifesat))               #3. sort: the most satisfied first

head(step3)

#This works, but it creates many "step" objects that we only need once.
##Next week we learn the PIPE, which chains these steps together without any extra objects.
```
